A central bank that reserves the right to surprise you is a central bank you position for honestly, with smaller bets. The howling from trading desks is the sound of a subsidy being repriced. It is also, not incidentally, the sound of a chair discovering that silence is the only tool that offends the White House and the bond market equally.

Because note what Warsh did not do today, in either direction. No hike, though his career's writings argue for one. No cut, though his patron demands it. A 9-3 hold, a statement acknowledging "elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East," and a refusal to promise anything about September. You can call it paralysis. You can also call it the only position from which the institution's independence survives the year, a chair proving to a hostile market and a hungrier White House that the committee, and only the committee, moves the rate. The most consequential thing about today may simply be that the president's chairman declined to deliver the president's rate cut, at a meeting where the live alternative was a hike.

One more mechanical note, the kind that never makes the recap videos. A war is the worst possible weather for a central bank because it breaks the tool. Oil at $78 because of missiles is inflation the funds rate cannot touch; the Fed can't print barrels, and hiking against a supply shock taxes the economy twice. The textbook says look through it. The 1970s say looking through it is how the anchor slips. The committee's split today is, at bottom, a disagreement about which of those two sentences carries the weight right now, and no PhD, and no lack of one, settles it. The models simply do not know. That, and no personality clash, is why the vote cracked.

So, markers, and this time the calendar is kind enough to be specific. Two inflation reports land before the committee reconvenes September 15-16. If they keep printing in the mid-3s, I say the dissenters win and the hike happens, the first in over three years, and the political explosion (a Trump-appointed chair raising rates into a midterm year) will be the finance story of the autumn. If inflation finally cracks lower, the hold holds, the doves exhale, and the two-hikes pricing dies quietly. Either way, watch one instrument for the verdict on all of it: the 30-year Treasury, which cares nothing for committee politics and prices only one thing, whether anyone still believes the long-run inflation promise. It has been drifting up all month, through today's decision, which is the bond market's way of clearing its throat.

Ninety-nine years ago this institution was invented so that one man's judgment would never again be the financial system's last line of defense. Today its nineteen judgments split three ways under one roof, which is either the system failing or the system working, and I keep coming back to the suspicion that it's both: the committee was built to average away conviction, and 2026 keeps sending it problems that refuse to be averaged.

Next meeting, someone has to be wrong out loud. September 16. Mark it.

Sources: FOMC statement and vote, July 29, 2026 (9-3 hold at 3.50–3.75%; Hammack, Kashkari, Logan dissents); market pricing via futures as of the July 29 close (September and December hikes); spring 2026 CPI and PPI prints (3.8% and 6.0%) per BLS releases; Kashkari dissent history, 2017–2019 FOMC records; Warsh confirmation and swearing-in, May 13 and May 22, 2026.

item.title: The One-Man Fed
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: The Federal Reserve's rate-setting committee meets on Tuesday and Wednesday: nineteen officials, hundreds of PhD economists in support, a communications…
item.content:encoded:
Sunday special edition

The Federal Reserve's rate-setting committee meets on Tuesday and Wednesday: nineteen officials, hundreds of PhD economists in support, a communications apparatus that weighs adverbs like plutonium. Ahead of that, I want to spend today on some history, because the Fed is young enough that you can meet the thing it replaced. The thing it replaced was one enormous, terrifying old man with a diseased nose, and the week he spent saving the American financial system is still the best crash course in what central banking actually is.

The library

Saturday night, November 2, 1907. New York has been in full financial panic for two weeks. The stock market has fallen by nearly half from its peak the year before. Depositors are queuing overnight outside trust companies, the era's shadow banks. Call-money rates on the exchange floor have touched 100 percent annualized. There is no central bank; America abolished its last one in 1836, on the theory that concentrated financial power was un-American, and has since run the fastest-growing economy on earth with no lender of last resort, no deposit insurance, and a currency supply with the flexibility of a cast-iron pipe.

What America has instead, at this particular moment, is John Pierpont Morgan, age 70, half-retired, summoned back from an Episcopal church convention in Richmond when the trouble started.

That Saturday night, Morgan gathers roughly fifty presidents of the city's trust companies in his private library on East 36th Street, marble, tapestries, Gutenberg Bibles, and tells them, in substance, that they will pool $25 million to save the weakest among them, because if they do not, Monday will destroy them all. The negotiations crawl. Sometime after midnight, Morgan closes the library door and puts the key in his pocket. Nobody leaves until the paper is signed. At 4:45 a.m., the senior trust president signs, and the rest follow.

Everyone knows that image; it's the most famous door in financial history. The part people skip is what happened before Morgan locked it, and the before is where all the actual content lives.

Two weeks earlier, when the panic first hit, the natural move was to save the first domino: the Knickerbocker Trust, third-largest in the city, run by a Morgan acquaintance, wobbling after its president was linked to a failed scheme to corner the copper market. Everyone begged Morgan to rescue it. He sent a young man named Benjamin Strong to go through Knickerbocker's books overnight, and when Strong reported that he could not certify the thing as solvent, Morgan let it die. It failed on October 22. Then the mob turned to the Trust Company of America, and Strong's examiners went through those books, and this time the answer was different: illiquid, yes; insolvent, no. Morgan's verdict, as recorded: then this is the place to stop the trouble.

Hold that pair of decisions in your mind. One institution allowed to fail, one saved, on the basis of an overnight forensic distinction between broke and merely busy. That distinction is the entire intellectual content of central banking. Everything since is elaboration.

The rest of the fortnight is a highlight reel of improvised authority. The city of New York, days from missing payroll: Morgan takes $30 million of its bonds. The stock exchange, about to close early because no one will lend against stocks: Morgan summons the bank presidents at 2 p.m. and raises $25 million in about ten minutes, and the exchange stays open. A Sunday comes, and he asks the city's clergy to preach calm; the sermons are, in effect, part of the financial plumbing that weekend. John D. Rockefeller deposits $10 million into the pool and tells reporters he'd give half of all he had to maintain America's credit. The US Treasury, for its part, deposits $35 million into national banks and then is tapped out; the Secretary of the Treasury essentially hands Morgan the keys and watches.

Note what Morgan is doing in functional terms. He is inventing, live, with his own and borrowed money, the machinery every modern crisis manager now runs by statute: emergency liquidity against collateral, triage between solvent and insolvent, coordination of private balance sheets, communication designed to break the psychology of the run. Walter Bagehot had written the recipe in 1873 (in a panic, lend freely, on good collateral, at a penalty rate), but Bagehot assumed a central bank would do it. In America the central bank was one mortal man with gout, working from a smoke-filled library, sustained on cigars and, during the worst nights, almost no sleep.

Why did it work? Because a panic, at its mechanical heart, is an information vacuum. Every bank borrows short and lends long, so no bank can survive all its depositors at once, so the only thing standing between any bank and death is the depositors' belief that other depositors aren't coming. In the vacuum, the rational move is to run first and ask later, and everyone runs. What stops it is a credible entity that can see inside the balance sheets and is willing to bet its own money on the difference between illiquid and insolvent. The Fed does this today with examiners and discount windows. In 1907 the credible entity was Morgan's eyes plus Strong's ledgers plus a reputation so heavy that his yes or no functioned as a clearing price. People trusted the verdict because the verdict was collateralized by Morgan's entire life.

The work

That reputation was not conjured for the occasion, and the résumé behind it is worth the tour, because Morgan's whole career was a single idea applied at increasing scale. The idea: unmanaged competition and unmanaged panic were the same disease (chaos, expensive to everyone) and his job was to impose order on both, whether or not anyone had asked him to.

He was born in Hartford in 1837, son of a transatlantic banker who drilled into him that a banker's capital is his good name. He spent a sickly childhood in and out of convalescence, and grew into a physique that did half his negotiating: over six feet, barrel-chested, with a rhinophyma-swollen nose he refused to fix and eyes that the photographer Edward Steichen, who shot the famous 1903 portrait where the chair's armrest gleams like a dagger, said were like staring into the headlights of an oncoming express train.

The signature work was the railroads. American railways in the Gilded Age were finance's Wild West: overbuilt, over-leveraged, run by buccaneers, permanently at war over rates, and serially bankrupt; by the mid-1890s something like a third of the nation's track mileage had passed through receivership. Morgan's firm made itself the emergency room. He would take a broken railroad, force the old shareholders to accept losses, cut the debt to what the traffic could actually pay, install his own men on the board through voting trusts, and end the rate wars by the simple expedient of making former combatants share directors. The press called it Morganization. It was the invention of modern restructuring, and also, less charmingly, the invention of engineering-away-competition, and both descriptions are accurate at once, which is the thing about Morgan you have to be able to hold.

The state, in this period, kept discovering that it needed him. In 1895 the US Treasury's gold reserve, the thing that made dollars credibly convertible, was draining toward nothing (below the statutory $100 million floor, heading for the point where the government literally could not pay in gold). President Cleveland, out of options, took a deal from Morgan and the Rothschilds' American agent: a private syndicate would deliver 3.5 million ounces of gold in exchange for bonds, executed through a forgotten Civil War statute Morgan himself dug up and put on the table. The syndicate propped the dollar, turned a profit doing it, and Congress spent years investigating; Morgan, asked at a hearing what he had expected to make, answered that he had been trying to save the country's credit and had not thought it his business to calculate. Believe him or don't. The gold arrived.

And in 1901 came the deal that still defines scale. Andrew Carnegie, ready to retire, scribbled his price on a slip of paper; Morgan glanced at it and said he accepted. The figure was $480 million for Carnegie Steel, and around it Morgan assembled United States Steel, capitalized at $1.4 billion: the first billion-dollar corporation, in an economy whose entire annual output was around $20 billion. As a share of the economy, imagine a single new company today capitalized somewhere north of a trillion and a half dollars, formed over a few weeks of meetings. When Morgan congratulated Carnegie on becoming the richest man in the world, he was, characteristically, announcing the score of a game he had just redesigned.

Character

The republic never decided how it felt about him, and the ambivalence was earned from both directions. The same man who stopped the 1907 panic used the panic to let U.S. Steel swallow a major Southern competitor, with a president's antitrust blessing extracted overnight while the market hung hostage. The same public that cheered the rescue then spent 1912 watching the Pujo Committee map the "money trust": Morgan partners and allies holding directorships across banks, railroads, and industrials that added up, by the committee's count, to influence over resources exceeding $22 billion, a number chosen to frighten and successful at it. The hearings produced the exchange he is remembered by. Asked by counsel whether commercial credit was based primarily upon money or property, Morgan answered: no, sir; the first thing is character. Money cannot buy it, he went on, because a man he did not trust could not get money from him on all the bonds in Christendom.

Cynics note that the man who said this had spent a career deciding, personally, who had character, with his own firm frequently on the profitable end of the verdict. Also true. But 1907 is the empirical test of whether the line was mere pose, and it wasn't: the entire rescue ran on exactly that faculty. Strong's ledgers could establish solvency. Only credibility could make fifty frightened trust presidents accept the finding at 4 a.m. and wire the money by Monday. The panic ended when Morgan's judgment became, briefly, the currency everyone agreed to clear in. That is what a lender of last resort is: an entity whose balance sheet and verdicts are trusted when nothing else is. In 1907, the balance sheet was adequate. The verdicts were the whole game.

He died sixteen months after Pujo, in his sleep at the Grand Hotel in Rome, on March 31, 1913, age 75. Wall Street flew flags at half-mast; the exchange he had kept open paused trading in his honor. His estate came to about $68 million outside the art, prompting Rockefeller's immortal, backhanded eulogy: and to think, he wasn't even a rich man.

Nine months later, in December 1913, Congress passed the Federal Reserve Act. The line from the library to the Act is direct and documented: the men who drafted the blueprint at their secret Jekyll Island retreat in 1910 included Morgan partners and allies, and the first head of the New York Fed, the operating heart of the new system, was Benjamin Strong, the same man who had gone through Knickerbocker's books overnight. America looked at the 1907 rescue, understood with perfect clarity that it had outsourced its monetary survival to the mortality and goodwill of one man, and built a bureaucracy to replace him. The one-man Fed became the Fed.

Replace, at least, in the org chart. Here is the thought I'd leave you with before Wednesday's meeting, and before an autumn that (between gated credit funds, a bond market asking fiscal questions, and a war with a dead ceasefire) may yet ask the old question again. Every acute crisis since 1913 has, at its worst hour, collapsed back into the library: a weekend, closed doors, a handful of people deciding which institutions are illiquid and which are insolvent, with imperfect ledgers and no time. Bear Stearns and Lehman were decided in rooms like that in 2008, one saved-ish, one let go, by officials openly haunted by which was which. The 2023 bank failures were resolved over a weekend of balance-sheet triage that Benjamin Strong would have recognized instantly, down to the overnight hours. We built the committee, the models, the statutes, and the acronyms precisely so that no one would ever again have to trust one man's eyes. And at every true extremity, what the system still runs on is some person, in some room, making Morgan's call with Morgan's information, minus the cigar.

The committee meets Wednesday. It will manage, with nineteen votes and four hundred economists, the ordinary weather. It exists because of the storms, and the storms have never once read the org chart.

Sources: contemporaneous accounts and standard histories of the Panic of 1907 (Bruner & Carr, "The Panic of 1907"; Strouse, "Morgan: American Financier"); Pujo Committee testimony, December 1912 (character exchange, money-trust tabulations); Treasury gold syndicate of 1895 records and congressional inquiries; U.S. Steel formation, 1901 (Carnegie sale, capitalization); Federal Reserve Act, December 23, 1913; Jekyll Island accounts per Vanderlip and later Fed histories.

item.title: The People Printing Money Are Buying Gold
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: On the last weekend of February 2022, while Russian tanks idled outside Kyiv, officials in Washington, Brussels, and Tokyo did something no one had ever done to…
item.content:encoded:
On the last weekend of February 2022, while Russian tanks idled outside Kyiv, officials in Washington, Brussels, and Tokyo did something no one had ever done to a great power. They froze the Central Bank of Russia's foreign reserves, roughly $300 billion, and almost none of it sat in any vault in Moscow. It existed as claims on Western institutions: Treasury bonds in custody accounts, deposits at Western banks, euros at Euroclear. Russia had spent two decades building a war chest. It turned out to be parked in the enemy's garage.

Every reserve manager on earth watched that weekend and learned the same lesson, which has nothing to do with Russia and everything to do with what money is. A reserve held in someone else's currency is a promise, and promises have an off switch, and the switch is in someone else's building. There is exactly one reserve asset with no off switch, no counterparty, no custodian who answers to a foreign ministry. It is a shiny yellow rock, and since that weekend, the world's central banks have been buying it at a pace unseen since the 1960s.

I bring this up now because gold is having the strangest year of any major asset, and you cannot understand the strangeness without the Moscow lesson. The strangeness comes in two facts that should not coexist.

Fact one: gold has crashed. After a historic melt-up that carried it from under $2,000 in late 2023 to a peak near $5,600 early this year, it has fallen back to around $4,000. It closed June at $4,018, down 14 percent for the second quarter alone, down more than a quarter from the top. Silver fell 22 percent last quarter. On July 8, the day Iranian missiles hit 85 targets across the Gulf and Brent jumped eight percent, gold went down 2.2 percent. Read that sentence twice. War broke out, and the war asset fell.

Fact two: the biggest, most deliberate buyers on the planet did not blink. On July 7, the People's Bank of China announced its twentieth consecutive monthly increase in gold reserves, adding about 15 tonnes in June, its largest monthly purchase of the current streak. Not despite the falling price. Visibly, cheerfully, into it. Buying the dip, as a matter of state policy.

So the price of gold is collapsing while the most sophisticated and least price-sensitive buyers in the world accelerate their purchases. Someone is selling urgently enough to overwhelm them. Today's essay is about who, and why, and what it tells you about an asset that, I'll argue, most people misread, including many of the people who own it.

Start with the misunderstanding, because everything else hangs off it. Gold produces nothing. No coupons, no dividends, no earnings calls. You cannot do to gold what we did to SpaceX two weeks ago, projecting cash flows and discounting them, because there are no cash flows to discount. An asset with no cash flows cannot be valued. It can only be priced, which means: it is worth what the next person will pay, full stop, and all analysis of gold is analysis of who the next person is.

This sounds like an insult. It's a classification, and it explains gold's behavior better than any inflation model. The question to ask about gold is never "what is it worth" (unanswerable) but "who is the marginal buyer and seller right now" (answerable, and profitable).

And the answer in 2026 is that gold has two almost completely separate markets wearing one price.

The first market is Western and financial. It trades gold: ETFs in London and New York, futures on COMEX, momentum funds, wealth managers sprinkling three percent into portfolios, retail buyers who watched the melt-up on their phones. In January, with the price near its peak, a Kitco survey found 71 percent of retail investors expected gold above $5,000 by year-end. That crowd owns gold on leverage and on feelings, marks it to market daily, and can be forced to sell by a margin clerk. To this market, gold is a trade with a chart.

The second market is Eastern and official. It accumulates gold: the PBoC, the central banks of the Gulf and Central Asia, institutions running the Moscow lesson through their reserve models. This crowd does not mark to market in any way that matters, publishes its purchases with a delay and a shrug, and measures position size in decades. To this market, gold is a fifty-year decision that happens to have a daily price: the only money that cannot be frozen by a Treasury official on a weekend.

Once you see the two markets, the 2026 crash resolves into something much more interesting than a crash. Walk the causes in order.

The melt-up itself was the first market at full sprint: momentum, ETF inflows, the 2025 fear trade around deficits and de-dollarization headlines, each price record generating the next buyer. Assets with no cash flows have no anchor, which means they overshoot in both directions; nothing says "stop" at $5,600 for the same reason nothing said "stop" at $2,000.

Then, over the spring, the first market's reasons evaporated one by one. The new Fed chair arrived in May with a hawkish reputation and a doctrine of less accommodation, and gold's oldest enemy is a credible central banker paying a real yield; every uptick in expected rates raises the cost of holding the asset that pays nothing. Inflation ran hot (3.8 percent CPI, 6 percent producer prices in the spring prints), which textbook logic says should help gold, and instead hurt it, because hot inflation now summons rate hikes, and the hikes hurt more than the inflation helps. The dollar strengthened. The June ceasefire subtracted the war premium. And when the tech selloff hit in late June, gold fell with the Nasdaq, because in a deleveraging, the safe asset is the ATM: you sell what has a bid to cover what doesn't. July 8 was the purest specimen. Missiles flew, margin calls landed, and gold funded them.

Every one of those forces operated on the first market. None of them touched the second. The PBoC does not care about Warsh's dot plot, has no margin clerk, and is executing a two-decade policy at whatever the London fix says today, where a lower fix simply means more tonnes per billion. Twenty months, no pause, biggest purchase of the streak into June's lows.

Which yields the cleanest way to describe 2026's gold market, and the sentence I'd keep from this essay: the crash and the accumulation are the same event, seen from opposite sides. The West's traders are selling gold to the East's states, urgently, at a discount, and the price is set by the urgency of the sellers while the ownership migrates to hands that will never give it back. Metal is leaving the map of things that trade and entering the map of things that sit in vaults for fifty years. Market people call this a bear market. A geologist would call it sequestration.

Does the migration matter? I think it matters more than almost anything else the price could tell you, for a reason that takes one more layer of ELI5.

Ask why a central bank, an institution whose entire product is paper money, hoards the one asset that competes with paper money. The Moscow lesson is the sharp answer, and there's a softer, older one underneath it: a reserve is supposed to be the thing that works when everything else doesn't. Treasuries work as long as Washington is your friend. Euros work as long as Brussels is. Gold works, period; its whole value proposition is indifference. It pays no interest precisely because it makes no promises, and a thing that makes no promises cannot break any. Central banks are not buying an investment. They are buying the absence of a counterparty: insurance against a world where the plumbing itself takes sides, written by the only insurer that never asks questions.

Seen that way, the streak through the crash is not stubbornness. An insurance buyer who stops paying premiums because insurance got cheaper has misunderstood his own program. The PBoC's June purchase at $4,000 and its purchases at $5,400 are the same decision; only the exchange rate between paper and indifference moved.

Now the falsifiable part, because an essay about an unanchored asset owes you markers.

First marker: the war test. The ceasefire is dead, the Gulf is burning again, and the strait's reopening is in doubt. If gold cannot reclaim and hold $4,500 with an actual shooting war running, then the old reflex (war, therefore gold) is finished for this cycle, and the first market's deleveraging still owns the tape. As of this morning gold sits near $4,050, and the reflex is on trial.

Second marker: the streak. Watch the PBoC's monthly announcement, first week of each month, the dullest press release in finance and currently the most informative. The streak surviving a 28 percent drawdown tells you the buyer is insensitive to price. If the streak ever stops on a price spike rather than a price fall, that tells you the insurance program has a budget after all. Twenty months in, no budget is visible.

Third: the arbitrage between the two markets has a tell. Physical premiums in Shanghai over the London price, and central-bank tonnage reported by the World Gold Council each quarter. If Western ETF outflows slow while official buying holds, the price finds its floor at whatever level the states are willing to absorb the West's remaining urgency, and I'd expect that floor to be violent, because insurance buyers with printing presses do not run out of money. They run out of sellers.

There's a version of this essay that ends with a prediction about the price, and I'm declining to write it, for the honest reason that unanchored assets make fools of anyone with a target. I'll end instead with the asymmetry that the whole year has exposed. The people selling gold in 2026 are selling because their charts broke, their margins called, their trades needed funding: reasons measured in days. The people buying are buying because they watched a $300 billion war chest evaporate over a weekend and resolved, at the level of national policy, never to be in that position: reasons measured in generations. Day-traders versus dynasties, and the dynasties are getting filled.

The price will tell you who's winning this week. The tonnage tells you who's winning the century.

Sources: Q2 2026 precious metals data (quarter open, April 14 peak $4,852, June 24 low, quarter close $4,018.74); 2026 peak and drawdown levels per market coverage of the spring correction; PBoC reserve announcements (July 7, 2026: 20th consecutive month, ~15 tonnes in June; Kitco, China Daily); Kitco retail survey, January 2, 2026 (71% above $5,000); July 8 session data (gold −2.24% to $4,066); Central Bank of Russia reserve freeze, February 2022, as reported at the time; World Gold Council quarterly demand series.

item.title: The Largest Refund in History
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: The largest financial operation of 2026 runs on CSV files.
item.content:encoded:
The largest financial operation of 2026 runs on CSV files.

Somewhere in a Customs and Border Protection system called CAPE, launched on April 20 with the fanfare of a printer-driver update, importers upload spreadsheets listing their customs entries, up to 9,999 rows per declaration, one row per shipment of sneakers or brake pads or garden gnomes. A declaration, once accepted, cannot be amended; get a tax ID wrong and you start over, which about 15 percent of early filers discovered the hard way. Files that clear are queued for payment, by ACH only, paper checks having been abolished in February. And through this contraption, the United States government is currently wiring back the better part of $175 billion in taxes that the Supreme Court says it should never have collected.

In June alone, $49.1 billion went out the door. That is the largest month of refunds in American history. By July 10, the running total hit $86.3 billion, with $121.75 billion of claims accepted for processing and roughly $80 billion still owed. For scale: the government is refunding, per month, more than it spends on NASA per year, and it is doing so with interest, compounded daily.

I want to walk through this machine today for two reasons. The obvious one is that it's a spectacular, under-covered story: the fiscal equivalent of a dam removal, with hedge funds circling and class-action lawyers filing and the Treasury bleeding from a wound inflicted by its own Constitution. The better one is that the refund is accidentally running the greatest economics experiment of the decade. For years, economists argued about who actually paid the Trump tariffs. Importers? Foreign exporters? American consumers? The argument was theoretical. Now $175 billion has to physically land in someone's bank account, and every dollar of it is a data point. We are about to find out who paid, by watching who fights hardest to get paid back.

The machine

Rewind quickly. In February, the Supreme Court decided Learning Resources v. Trump (the lead plaintiff, delightfully, a family-owned educational toy company from Illinois) and struck down the tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act: the "Liberation Day" duties, the fentanyl-justified ones, the reciprocal schedules. The Court's reasoning, compressed: IEEPA lets a president regulate commerce in an emergency, and a permanent, revenue-raising tariff wall is a tax, and taxes belong to Congress. Whatever your politics, note what the ruling did fiscally. Roughly $164.7 billion had been collected under IEEPA authority by January. That money was now, legally speaking, not the government's.

Governments have owed money before. What makes this episode strange is the mechanics of owing it back to hundreds of thousands of importers, entry by entry, with statutory interest running at 6 percent for corporations and 7 percent for individuals, compounded daily, under a customs regulation written for ordinary billing disputes. Compounded daily is not a phrase that usually appears next to eleven-figure sums. While the refunds crawl, the meter runs at junk-bond rates. The federal government has spent 2026 as the most creditworthy borrower on earth paying some of the worst rates in America, on a loan it never meant to take, from lenders who never meant to make it.

And the crawl matters, because the machine has a sequencing problem that will surprise no one who has ever dealt with a large institution. The first, cleanest payments went to the biggest, best-lawyered filers; Walmart and Ford were reportedly among the early recipients, their entries filed clean, their banking details in order. Meanwhile roughly 70 percent of smaller importers are still waiting, thousands of approved claims are stuck on invalid bank details, and an $11.4 billion pile of older entries waits for a later phase of the system. This month the Court of International Trade added a twist with an order whose practical meaning, per the trade bar, is that importers who actually sued get made whole fastest, while everyone who politely waited stands in the administrative queue. The government, for its part, is appealing the refund order even as it pays, a posture best described as writing checks while arguing you shouldn't have to.

If you want a one-line summary of the machine: the money is flowing, the interest is compounding, and the speed of your justice is a function of the quality of your paperwork.

The market

Now the fun part. Wherever there is a large pot of money arriving at an uncertain date, finance will manufacture a way to sell the waiting.

Within weeks of the ruling, a secondary market in tariff refund claims had formed, estimated as large as $100 billion in face value. The trade is simple. You are an importer owed $20 million someday. A fund offers you cash now for the claim, or a loan against it at about 50 cents of advance per dollar of claim, minimum size $10 million, interest accruing in kind. The buyers are hedge funds and, inevitably, private credit funds, an industry currently gating its own investors (see Saturday's essay) while raising money to buy receivables from the United States government.

The pricing history of these claims is the part I'd frame and hang on a wall. Before the Supreme Court ruled, refund claims changed hands at around 20 cents on the dollar. After the ruling: up to 60 cents. Which means that before February, the sharpest money in the country was pricing the odds that the Supreme Court would strike down the tariffs at something like one in five, net of waiting costs, and you could trade that opinion. Constitutional law had a price, updated continuously, posted in a market almost nobody knew existed. The law schools teach doctrine. The claims desks were running a prediction market on it, with nine-figure stakes.

Why only 60 cents even now, with the government literally paying? Because the fine print is a minefield, and the fine print is where this story gets almost baroquely good. A Civil War-era statute, the Assignment of Claims Act, makes selling a claim against the government legally awkward until the claim is formally allowed and warranted, so the funds structure around it with liens and proceeds interests of contested strength. If the importer goes bankrupt before its customs entries are reliquidated, the refund might legally be born after the bankruptcy filing, potentially cutting the lender out entirely; no court has yet decided when, exactly, a tariff refund becomes property. Some importers' own credit agreements contain sweep clauses that grab extraordinary receipts and force them into debt prepayment, meaning the refund arrives and immediately leaves for the benefit of a lender who read the documents more carefully than anyone else. Sixty cents is what certainty about the government's debt looks like after subtracting uncertainty about everything else.

Who paid

Which brings us to the deepest layer, the one that turns this from a plumbing story into an economics experiment.

The refunds go to importers, because importers are who legally paid. Cue the obvious scream: wait, the importers passed the tariff on to us. And so, right on schedule, consumer class actions have been filed against refund-collecting importers, on theories of unjust enrichment, arguing the companies raised prices to cover the tariffs and would now be paid twice. Business customers are combing their supply contracts for surcharge and change-in-law clauses to claw back their share. The trade bar is openly advising claim buyers that the gross refund from CBP "may not equal the net value retained," which is lawyer for: expect to share.

The fight underneath rests on a concept worth more than most finance degrees, so let's have it in plain terms. Who pays a tax has two answers: the legal one (who writes the check) and the economic one (whose prices and wages end up worse). They are almost never the same person. Put a levy on importers and the importer writes the check, then tries to recover it: charge customers more, squeeze the foreign supplier for a discount, eat thinner margins. How the burden splits depends on who can least afford to walk away, and economists studying the 2018-2025 tariffs found, over and over, that foreign exporters barely budged their prices, which means the burden landed almost entirely inside America, split between company margins and consumer prices, in proportions that vary by product and remain fought over in the journals.

The refund now has to run that film backwards. The check goes to the legal payer. The economic payers, armed with subpoenas, want their share back out of it. Which means American courtrooms are about to spend years computing, product by product, invoice by invoice, the very pass-through rates that the economics profession could only estimate in aggregate. The tariff, in death, will produce better data on tariff incidence than it ever did in life. Somewhere, a graduate student is going to build a career on the discovery documents.

Step back and look at the fiscal picture, because it connects to everything else this newsletter has been tracking. The deficit was already tracking past $2 trillion this year. Subtract the tariff revenue that vanished with the ruling (IEEPA duties were more than half of all customs collections in January), add $175 billion of refunds with daily-compounding interest, add a war's worth of spending, and you begin to understand why the fiscal argument has stopped being a think-tank pastime and started showing up in bond auctions. The Treasury is simultaneously refunding a tax, fighting the refund on appeal, and borrowing to fund both the refund and the fight. On the country's 250th birthday I wrote that the auctions define "excessive" one Tuesday at a time. Add this: sometimes the Supreme Court gets a vote too.

The marker I'll put down: the refund story's second act is nastier than its first. Act one was mechanical (file the CSV, receive the wire). Act two is distributional, and distribution fights are where the knives come out: importer versus customer, claim-buyer versus bankruptcy trustee, the government versus its own obligation, appeal pending, interest compounding daily in the background like a taxi meter nobody can find the off switch for. By my arithmetic the interest alone on the unpaid balance is accruing at something like $13 million a day. The toy company won. The lawyers, as ever, won bigger. And the question the whole episode leaves standing is the one it started with, now with empirical stakes: when a government taxes imports, who truly pays? The answer, being assembled right now in a thousand dockets: everyone, in shares to be determined, with interest.

Sources: Penn Wharton Budget Model, Supreme Court tariff ruling analysis, February 2026 ($164.7B collected, refund and revenue projections); CBP CAPE system notices and trade-bar summaries (April–July 2026); refund tallies as of July 10, 2026 ($86.3B paid; $49.1B in June; interest under 19 CFR 24.36); Sidley Austin, claims-market analysis, April 2026 (secondary market size, 20-to-60-cent pricing, lending structures, Assignment of Claims Act and bankruptcy risks); Holland & Knight and Morgan Lewis client alerts on the CIT refund orders and the government's June appeal; consumer class-action filings as reported spring 2026.

item.title: Your Money Is Fine, You Just Can't Have It
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: Say you put $500,000 into Blackstone's flagship private credit fund, BCRED, sometime in the boom.
item.content:encoded:
Say you put $500,000 into Blackstone's flagship private credit fund, BCRED, sometime in the boom. It was an easy sale: a 9-plus percent yield, a portfolio of senior secured loans to solid American companies, statements that arrived every month showing a net asset value that basically never went down. Bonds without the mood swings. Your financial adviser probably owned it too.

This spring you decided you'd like some of the money back. Maybe the yield on plain Treasuries got competitive, maybe tuition came due, maybe the headlines about private credit started using words like "reckoning" and you decided you'd read enough. You submitted your redemption request like roughly ten percent of the fund's shareholders did in the second quarter, $4.4 billion of requests in all.

The fund sent back about 45 cents of each requested dollar, with a note explaining the rest would have to wait. On June 4, for the first time in its history, Blackstone had invoked the gate: a clause, sitting in the prospectus all along, capping total redemptions at 5 percent of the fund per quarter. Nothing was violated. Everything worked precisely as documented. Your money is fine, the marks say so, and you cannot have it.

Today's essay is about that clause, the trillion-and-a-half-dollar industry built on top of it, and the oldest trick in finance, which the clause was designed to survive. Because here is the sentence I want you to carry out of this piece: private credit did not invent a new asset class. It reinvented the bank, minus the deposit insurance, and this year the depositors started asking for their money.

The bank costume

Strip the branding and look at the machine. BCRED gathers money from hundreds of thousands of individuals who expect, within reason, to be able to get it back. It takes that money and makes loans to companies, loans that cannot be sold quickly or easily, at a markup. It layers on borrowed money of its own (about $36 billion of debt against $45 billion of investor capital, a leverage ratio of 0.8 times) to juice the yield. Collect deposits, hold illiquid loans, lever the book, pay depositors a spread. That is a bank. That has been the definition of a bank since Renaissance Italy.

And banks have one ancient failure mode. The loans come due in years; the depositors can ask today. If too many ask at once, the bank must sell loans fast, fast selling means bad prices, bad prices mean the last depositors out get less than whole, which is why everyone races to be first, which is the run. It is the most reliable catastrophe in financial history. Every structure that borrows short and lends long carries it like a gene.

Civilization's answer, after the 1930s burned half the American banking system down, was a bargain: banks got deposit insurance and a central bank willing to lend against good collateral in a panic, and in exchange they accepted examiners, capital rules, and limits on what they could hold. Runs mostly stopped. The bargain held for ninety years.

Private credit's founding insight was that you could have the bank without the bargain. No deposit insurance, no Fed backstop, no examiners second-guessing your marks. In exchange for giving all that up, you need some other answer to the run. Their answer is the gate. You cannot have a run if the depositors are contractually forbidden from running. Five percent per quarter, single file, no shoving.

I want to be fair to the design, because the design is clever. A gated fund cannot be forced into fire sales; it simply stops paying out. In a strict engineering sense the gate is a better run-stopper than deposit insurance, which merely discourages the stampede rather than banning it. The people who built these vehicles will tell you, correctly, that the gate is the product working as intended, disclosed on page whatever, initialed by every buyer.

All true. The trouble is what the existence of the gate does to the promise that sold the product. The pitch was bond-like income with bank-like stability. The reality, now visible, is bond-like income with hotel-California liquidity, and an exit that narrows at exactly the moment you want it. Liquidity is like oxygen in this specific way: its market price is approximately zero right up until the moment it is approximately infinite.

The marks

Now the part of the story I find most interesting, which is the question of what the money you cannot withdraw is actually worth.

BCRED reports a net asset value per share. That figure was $24.79 in December, $24.19 in March, $23.94 at the end of May: a stately, dignified 3.4 percent decline for the year. On the same statements, the portfolio's ingredients were moving less politely. Loans on non-accrual (the industry's term for borrowers who have stopped paying) jumped from 0.6 percent of the book at cost in the first quarter to 2.4 percent in the second. Quadrupled, in ninety days. A $1.1 billion loan to the software company Medallia is marked at 60 cents on the dollar. A position in Affordable Care fell to 70. The July distribution was cut to 18 cents a share, the second cut in nine months; it was 22 cents a year ago.

Hold those two pictures side by side. The headline NAV glides down a few percent a year, the way an administrator would draw it. The underlying book is producing quadrupling non-accruals and sixty-cent marks. Both come from the same building. The difference between the pictures is that nothing in the portfolio trades, so the value of everything is, within professional bounds, an opinion. The industry's critics have a name for the serenity this produces; the investor Cliff Asness has spent years calling it volatility laundering. The loans are just as risky as public credit, often riskier. What's been removed is the reporting of the risk.

If you want to know what happens when an actual market price intrudes on this arrangement, the industry provided a demonstration in the first quarter, and it is the single most clarifying number in this entire essay. Investors in Blue Owl's OTIC, a smaller non-traded vehicle, requested redemption of 40.7 percent of the fund. What the sellers who found exits received, in a secondary transaction, was 12 cents on the requested dollar of face. The statement says par-ish. The exit said twelve cents. Between a mark and a market there is sometimes a gap, and the gap is where careers, retirements, and lawsuits live.

To be scrupulously clear: BCRED is not OTIC. Blackstone's fund is enormous, 95 percent senior secured, has returned 9.8 percent annually since inception, and its 2.2 times interest coverage says the average borrower still earns its payments twice over. The system's defenders point to all of this, accurately. The reply, which 2026 keeps writing in larger font, is that averages are how credit trouble hides. Non-accruals quadrupling is not an average misbehaving. It is the tail arriving.

Where the run went

The industry-wide numbers say the tail has company. Across the non-traded funds, investors asked for $13.9 billion back in the first quarter; $4.6 billion of it was gated. New fundraising, the inflow side that made every prior exit painless, fell 74 percent in April from a year earlier. That last number deserves a beat of silence, because these vehicles were engineered around a current: money in the front, money out the back, the gate never needed as long as the front door stayed busy. The front door has gone quiet. What remains is a $79 billion portfolio, a queue at the back, and arithmetic.

Two threads make this bigger than one industry's awkward year.

First: who ends up owning these loans. The same managers running the retail funds also run private credit for insurance companies, which have loaded annuity portfolios (the thing your grandmother's retirement check comes out of) with exactly this paper, because the accounting treats unquoted assets gently. And the banks that were supposedly disrupted by private credit turn out to be its lenders: a large share of fund leverage, including a chunk of that $36 billion, is bank credit lines. The risk left the regulated system through the front door and re-entered through the loading dock, wearing a costume. Regulators spent fifteen years congratulating themselves that the banks were safe. The question of 2026 is what the banks are safe from, exactly, if they financed the thing that replaced them.

Second: why the borrowers are wobbling now. Read the names going bad and a pattern shows up. Medallia: enterprise software. A striking share of the loans souring across these books were 2021-vintage lending to software and services companies, the kind with recurring revenue that private credit considered the safest collateral on earth. Recurring, it turns out, means recurring until your customer replaces you, and 2026's corporate software budgets are being rewritten by AI at a pace nobody's covenant models contemplated. The safest collateral of the last cycle is the disruption surface of this one. I'll have much more to say about the AI unwind in a few weeks, but note the connection now: the same force deflating the Nasdaq's dreams is quietly defaulting the loans inside America's retirement products.

So, the markers I'd put down. Blackstone's own precedent, the BREIT property-fund gate of November 2022, took 18 months to lift, and that was with the Nasdaq roaring and rate cuts hoped for. BCRED's gate, in my judgment, outlasts BREIT's unless the default tide turns within two quarters, and the number that tells you is non-accruals in the Q3 report this autumn: under 2 percent, the machine restabilizes; anywhere near 4, the queue at the back door doubles and the distribution gets cut a third time. And watch for the year's quietest important trade: publicly traded BDCs already price at deep discounts to stated NAV, which means the stock market has already voted on what the marks are worth. The gate can stop the depositors. It cannot stop the repricing.

None of this required anyone to lie. That's what I find most instructive about it. Every clause was disclosed, every mark defensible, every yield real while it lasted. The industry simply rebuilt the oldest machine in finance, told everyone it was something new, and trusted that the tide would never ask everyone the same question on the same day. Banking's entire history is the story of that question eventually getting asked. This time the answer, printed politely at the bottom of half a million account statements, is: five percent per quarter, and thank you for your patience.

Sources: BCRED public disclosures and monthly NAV reports (December 2025 through May 2026); redemption and gating figures as reported June–July 2026 (Q2 requests $4.4B, June 4 gate, 5% cap); AltsWire, July 2026 distribution cut; sector redemption and fundraising data, Q1–Q2 2026 ($13.9B requests, $4.6B gated, April fundraising −74%); Blue Owl OTIC secondary pricing as reported spring 2026; Cliff Asness, "volatility laundering" commentaries, AQR; BREIT gating timeline, November 2022 onward.

item.title: Factories Without Customers
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: This morning in Beijing, the National Bureau of Statistics released two numbers that cannot both describe a healthy economy.
item.content:encoded:
This morning in Beijing, the National Bureau of Statistics released two numbers that cannot both describe a healthy economy.

The first: China's GDP grew 4.3 percent in the second quarter, the weakest reading since the end of 2022, when the country was still welding people into their apartments. It missed the consensus forecast, missed Beijing's own 4.5-to-5 percent target band, and marked a hard deceleration from 5 percent growth just one quarter earlier.

The second: exports in June were up 27 percent from a year ago.

Read those together. The overall economy is losing speed even though the part of it that sells to foreigners is growing at a pace normally associated with startups. Which means the part of it that sells to Chinese people is doing something much worse than 4.3 percent. And it is. Retail sales grew 1 percent in June, the third weak month in a row. Fixed-asset investment fell 5.7 percent in the first half. Property investment, the engine that once drove a quarter of Chinese economic activity, fell 18 percent, in year five of a decline that has now outlasted most marriages.

One country, two economies. The factories are sprinting. The households are hiding. Today's essay is about why that gap exists, why it is widening, and why the standard prescription (announce stimulus, wait, repeat) keeps failing to close it. Along the way I want to hand you the single most useful piece of arithmetic for reading any economy, because China right now is the clearest live demonstration of it on earth.

The arithmetic is this. Everything an economy produces has to be bought by someone. There are only four candidates: households (consumption), businesses and builders (investment), the government (spending), and foreigners (net exports). GDP is just the sum of the four. This sounds too simple to be useful, and it is the most useful sentence in macroeconomics, because it means that when one buyer disappears, the output they used to absorb has exactly three places to go, or it doesn't get produced, and somebody loses a job.

Run China through it. For thirty years, the second buyer did superhuman work: investment, above 40 percent of GDP, year after year, a share no large economy had ever sustained. Highways, ports, and above all apartments. Housing became the national savings account. Chinese households, with capital controls locking them out of foreign assets and a stock market that behaves like a casino with characteristics, put roughly two-thirds of their wealth into property. Developers borrowed against tomorrow's pre-sold apartments to build today's, local governments funded themselves by selling land to those developers, and everyone's balance sheet ended up resting on the same bet.

That bet broke in 2021, and the arithmetic has been grinding through the economy ever since. When property investment falls 18 percent, the first buyer of Chinese output (the construction complex) shrinks. Fine, says the textbook: households can pick up the slack. Except the same crash that idled the builders vaporized the households' net worth, because the apartments were the net worth. A family whose flat has lost a third of its value does not feel like shopping. It feels like saving, and that is what Chinese households are doing, relentlessly, in a way that no interest-rate cut has budged.

There's a name for this and it comes from Japan. The economist Richard Koo, watching Tokyo after its 1990 bust, called it a balance-sheet recession: the condition where households and firms, staring at damaged balance sheets, redirect income from spending to debt repair, and keep doing it whatever the central bank does, because you cannot rate-cut someone into feeling rich. Money gets cheaper; nobody wants it; the economy runs below capacity for years while everyone quietly heals. Japan needed the better part of two decades. China is in roughly year five, with a property overhang larger than Japan's was relative to its economy, and with one advantage Japan never had and one disadvantage Japan never faced.

The advantage is state control of the banks, which means no Lehman moment, no sudden cascade; the losses get socialized slowly, held on balance sheets at fictional marks, amortized across decades. The Chinese system does not do crashes. It does erosion.

The disadvantage is scale. Japan in 1995 was about 8 percent of the world economy and could export its way through its lost decades without anyone much minding. China is triple that share, and when it points its industrial machine outward, the world minds.

Which brings us to the 27 percent, because that number is the opposite of what it looks like. It looks like strength. It is the third buyer stepping in for the missing first two. When domestic consumption and investment cannot absorb what the factories produce, the output goes abroad, at whatever price it takes. Chinese electric vehicles, solar panels, batteries, steel, chemicals, machine tools: the export surge is the mirror image of the domestic collapse, the same overcapacity wearing its outbound uniform. Prices tell you it is a push, and China's producer prices have spent years in deflation. This is what it looks like when a $18 trillion economy tries to sell its surplus into a world that did not order it.

And 2026 handed that surplus a strange gift. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down the bulk of the American tariff wall, the IEEPA tariffs, on constitutional grounds. Whatever the domestic American politics of that decision, its trade meaning was immediate: the tax on Chinese goods entering their largest rich-world market fell sharply just as Chinese factories most needed somewhere to send output. Some of June's 27 percent is exactly that, cargo surging through a gate that a court unexpectedly propped open. The pushback will come from elsewhere, and it has already started: emerging economies from Brazil to India, watching their own manufacturers get undercut, have been raising trade barriers against Chinese goods all year. The next trade war will be less Washington versus Beijing, and more everyone versus overcapacity.

So why doesn't Beijing just fix it? The prescription is not mysterious, and every economist you ask recites the same one, including Cornell's Eswar Prasad, who summarized this week's data with the observation that China's economy "is becoming increasingly unbalanced": frontier-technology investment booming, consumption depressed. Give money to households. Build the pension and healthcare systems so families don't need to self-insure by hoarding savings. Accept slower headline growth with a healthier mix.

The answer to "why not" is that the imbalance is a policy, and behind it stands a worldview. The Chinese leadership has spent years signaling distrust of what it calls welfarism, the suspicion that direct transfers breed idleness, and a conviction that national strength lives in production, in factories and technology and export share, rather than in consumption. Money aimed at the economy keeps landing on the supply side: cheap credit for manufacturers, subsidies for priority industries, capacity, capacity, capacity. Each round makes the factories stronger and the glut worse. Stimulus that never touches the missing buyer cannot revive the missing buying.

Watch the Politburo's late-July economic meeting with that lens. The expectations run to targeted fiscal support, maybe consumption vouchers, accelerated local bond issuance. The tell will be the direction of the money. If it flows to households as spendable income, mark it as the turn, a genuine change of doctrine. If it flows, once again, to producers and projects, then the 27 percent gets larger, the 1 percent stays small, and the erosion continues on schedule. My money, with no joy in it, is on the second.

One more thing, the part I find quietly historic. For three decades, every Western business plan for China rested on a single sentence: a billion consumers are coming. The consumers arrived, briefly, in the 2010s, and then the property bust un-invited them. What exists now is the inversion of the dream: a country that produces like the future and consumes like the past, year five of a repair that outside estimates put closer to its beginning than its end. An urban unemployment rate of 5 percent and disposable income growing 5.2 percent sound respectable on paper, and are, and are also beside the point, because the issue was never income. It is the balance sheet, and balance sheets heal at the speed of fear.

Japan's version of this story ended, eventually, with corporate reform, a tourism boom, inflation imported at last, and a stock market that took 34 years to reclaim its 1989 high. Nikkei 38,915, December 1989; Nikkei 38,915 again, February 2024. Thirty-four years, round trip, for the patient.

The Shanghai Composite's all-time high is 6,124, set in October 2007. It trades today at roughly half that. If the balance-sheet playbook holds, somewhere out there is a February morning in the 2040s when Chinese state television gets to announce the recovery of a number first printed when the iPhone was four months old.

The factories will still be running. The question, then as now, is who buys.

Sources: National Bureau of Statistics Q2 2026 release as reported July 15, 2026 (GDP 4.3%, retail 1%, FAI −5.7%, property −18%, exports +27%, industrial production 5.3%); consensus and target-band context via ING and wire coverage; Eswar Prasad commentary, July 2026; Richard Koo, "The Holy Grail of Macroeconomics" (balance-sheet recession framework); Nikkei and Shanghai Composite index histories.

item.title: Mars, Discounted Daily
