item.description: In December, SpaceX ran an insider share sale that valued the company at $800 billion.
item.content:encoded:
In December, SpaceX ran an insider share sale that valued the company at $800 billion. Six months later, on June 11, it sold stock to the public at $135 a share, implying roughly $1.5 trillion. By the close of the first trading day, June 12, the ticker SPCX stood at $161, a 19 percent pop, and the company that had been worth $800 billion at Christmas was worth about $1.79 trillion by the following summer solstice.

One month on, the pop is gone. The stock has spent this week drifting back down through the $140s, pushed by the same two forces squeezing everything else with an AI story attached (a tech selloff that started in June, and a war that un-paused on Tuesday), and it is now knocking on its own IPO price from above.

So in seven months, the market's answer to the question "what is SpaceX worth" has been: $800 billion, then $1.5 trillion, then $1.79 trillion, then maybe $1.5 trillion again, and the company itself did approximately nothing in that time except continue being SpaceX. Launches launched. Starlink signed up subscribers. No new physics. The rockets are the same rockets; the number under them moved by a trillion dollars, twice, in both directions.

If that strikes you as strange, good. That strangeness is the most educational thing in markets right now, and today I want to use it to explain the single most useful idea in finance, which is also the most quietly radical: the difference between what something trades for and what it is worth. The best living guide to that difference, NYU's Aswath Damodaran, published a full valuation of SpaceX in April, before the IPO, and his numbers give us something almost unheard of in a mania: a benchmark that was written down in advance.

The machine that discounts

First, the idea, built from a lemonade stand, because I promised myself this newsletter would always be willing to go all the way down to the studs.

Your kid runs a lemonade stand. It reliably clears $100 every summer. What's the stand worth? Well: $100 next summer, but a dollar promised in a year is worth a bit less than a dollar in your hand (you could have banked today's dollar and earned interest, and also, the kid might quit). So you shave next summer's $100 down to, say, $93. Summer after that, shave twice. Add up every future summer, each one shaved harder than the last, and the pile of shaved dollars is what the stand is worth today. That's a discounted cash flow. That's the whole thing. Every valuation model on Wall Street is that arithmetic wearing progressively more expensive clothing.

Two dials control everything. How big the future cash flows get (the story dial), and how hard you shave them (the doubt dial). All financial screaming, everywhere, forever, is people disagreeing about one dial or the other.

Now watch what happens when the lemonade stand is a rocket company.

Damodaran's April valuation did exactly what the lemonade math demands, just with better ingredients. He broke SpaceX into its actual businesses and gave each one a story with numbers attached. The launch business, which currently moves more than 80 percent of everything humanity sends to orbit: he projected it to about $70 billion of revenue by 2036 with 40 percent operating margins. Starlink, the satellite broadband arm and already the bulk of current revenue: $100 billion by 2036 at 60 percent margins. The xAI piece, folded into the company this year: $80 billion at 50 percent. Then a bucket for the dreams with unclear invoices (space tourism, whatever Mars is commercially) at another $50 billion. Discount the whole thing at an 8 percent doubt dial and you get a value of about $1.22 trillion. He ran the model 10,000 times with the dials jittered randomly; the median came out at $1.29 trillion.

Pause on what those inputs concede. They concede near-monopoly in launch, forever-dominance in satellite internet, a successful AI business, and margins that almost no industrial company in history sustains, and the answer still comes out at $1.22 trillion. Against that: the IPO asked $1.5 trillion, and day-one buyers paid $1.79 trillion.

For scale, SpaceX's actual 2025 financials were about $15.6 billion of revenue and roughly $8 billion of EBITDA. At the day-one close, the market was paying around 81 times revenue and 156 times EBITDA. One hundred fifty-six years of current cash earnings, for a company whose main product operates on top of controlled explosions. The optimists' answer is that current earnings are irrelevant because the future is enormous, and the honest response is: correct, that is exactly the bet, now say it with the number attached. At $1.79 trillion you were not buying SpaceX the going concern. You were buying Damodaran's most generous scenario, plus a tip.

The two prices

Which returns us to the trillion-dollar wobble, because here's the naive question I promised: how does the same company get marked at $800 billion in December and $1.79 trillion in June? Nothing about the rockets changed. What changed?

The buyer changed.

December's $800 billion was a price set by insiders and funds in a private sale: patient money, negotiated access, spreadsheets out. June's $1.79 trillion was set at the margin by whoever wanted 100 shares badly enough at 9:31 a.m., which included, by all accounts, an enormous retail wave for whom SPCX was less a security than a souvenir. The first crowd was pricing a business. The second was pricing a story they wanted to be part of, and pricing it against nothing, because what is the comparable for Mars?

This is Damodaran's oldest distinction, and it carries the whole episode: valuing is estimating what the cash flows justify; pricing is guessing what the next person will pay. Both are real activities. Both can pay. But only one of them has a floor under it, and you find out which crowd you bought from on the days the story wobbles. The past month, with the stock sliding from $161 toward $135 on no rocket-specific news whatsoever, is what it looks like when the souvenir buyers finish buying and the marginal shareholder starts asking spreadsheet questions again.

There's a governance wrinkle that the pricing crowd mostly waved through, and it deserves a paragraph of its own. Elon Musk owns about 42 percent of the economics of SpaceX and controls roughly 80 percent of the votes. Buying SPCX is buying a minority, non-voting seat on a vehicle steered entirely by one man, a man whose defining corporate habit is bolting his ventures together (xAI is now inside the rocket company, a sentence I encourage you to read twice). Damodaran, who has been publicly fond of Musk's companies for years, put it about as gently as the facts permit: hard company to buy, dangerous company to short. Both clauses matter.

The index question

Now the subplot that I think becomes the main plot within a year or two, and it connects to something I wrote last Saturday about who shows up at Treasury auctions.

The S&P 500's rules say a company must be listed for at least a year, with adequate float and four profitable quarters, before it can join the index. SpaceX therefore can't enter before mid-2027 at the earliest, and OpenAI and Anthropic, still private but each flirting with trillion-dollar marks, can't enter at all. There is now open pressure on S&P to bend these rules, and Damodaran's June essay on the fight had a line I haven't stopped thinking about: S&P needs these companies in its index more than they need to be in it. An index claiming to represent American large-cap equity, while excluding two or three of the largest caps in America, has a product problem.

Why does anyone care so much? Because index inclusion is the last remaining source of automatic buying in the entire financial system. The S&P 500 constituents represent something like $63 trillion of float-adjusted market cap, shadowed by trillions of passive dollars that buy whatever the committee blesses, at whatever the price is that day, with the price-sensitivity of a tide. Every 401(k) contribution in a target-date fund is a standing order to purchase the index's members, sight unseen. Getting added is getting plumbed into everyone's paycheck.

A theme is developing in these essays: markets keep replacing discretionary buyers with mechanical ones, and then acting surprised by the consequences. Last week's essay was about the Treasury market losing its price-insensitive buyers. Equities ran the film in the other direction: the price-insensitive buyer took over. When SPCX eventually joins the index, a slug of it goes into every retirement account in the country automatically, no spreadsheet consulted, at 156 times whatever the multiple is that morning.

Worth remembering, while everyone lobbies: the inclusion pop itself is mostly a ghost. Damodaran's review of the evidence finds the bump from joining the S&P has shrunk decade by decade and has "largely disappeared" in recent years. Tesla, the loudest precedent and the closest cousin, joined in December 2020 amid euphoria and then underperformed the index it had just joined. The prize everyone is fighting over may be a trophy that stopped conferring anything years ago, which would make it a perfect emblem of this whole episode.

The number I'd write down

So what's the takeaway, with the stock hovering around its IPO price and the tape ugly?

Write down $110. That's roughly where Damodaran's base-case $1.22 trillion lands per share, and it's the most useful single number in this story, because it was computed before the listing, by someone with no position to defend, using assumptions that already grant SpaceX almost everything. Above it, you are paying for outcomes beyond his most generous line items; at it, you're paying for mere spectacular success; well below it, and the sober spreadsheet says the rocket company is cheap, which is a sentence that rarely stays true for long.

The stock will get its stress test soon enough. The IPO lockup expires in early August, releasing early holders to sell into whatever market August provides, and August is providing wars and a tech unwind. My marker, and you may hold me to it: SPCX trades through $135 and spends time in the low hundreds before Labor Day, at which point the same commentators calling it the people's rocket in June will call it a cautionary tale, and both takes will be exactly as lazy. The company was never worth $1.79 trillion and was never worth $800 billion either, and the distance between those numbers was never about rockets. It was the going rate for a story, quoted twice, to two different crowds.

The rockets, to their credit, keep flying. Rockets are the only part of this that was ever indifferent to the ticker, and there is a lesson in the fact that they are also the only part that works.

Sources: Damodaran, "To Trillion(s) and Beyond: A SpaceX IPO Odyssey" (April 23, 2026) and "SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic: The S&P 500 Inclusion Question" (June 18, 2026); CNBC IPO-day coverage, June 12, 2026 (pricing, first-day close); insider-sale valuation via Bloomberg/Business Standard, December 2025; CNBC, July 13-week coverage of the slide toward the IPO price; S&P Dow Jones index methodology (seasoning and profitability rules).

item.title: The People Who Price a War by Lunchtime
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: The news this morning is that the ceasefire is dead.
item.content:encoded:
The news this morning is that the ceasefire is dead. Iran fired on three tankers in the Strait of Hormuz yesterday, on the theory that they had failed to comply with what Tehran now calls its control of the passage. Washington reinstated oil sanctions. American aircraft hit Iranian coastal targets at Qeshm, Bandar Abbas, and Sirik overnight; Iran answered with strikes on 85 American-allied sites across Bahrain and Kuwait. The president, asked about the memorandum his own negotiators signed three weeks ago, said "as far as I'm concerned, it's over."

Brent jumped from $72 to $78 by breakfast. Seoul fell more than 5 percent. Tokyo lost 2. So did Mumbai. Four days ago, in this newsletter, I wrote that the futures market had priced the war at zero and that the tarp over it had a date printed on it. I did not expect to be proven right in under a week, and I take no satisfaction in it, partly because people are being shot at, and partly because there was a market that got this far more right than I did, and today's essay is about them.

While the futures strip spent June declaring peace, there was a group of professionals, most of them working within a few hundred meters of each other in the City of London, who never signed off on it. They don't trade oil. They price the ships that carry it, one voyage at a time, and their prices never came back down. This morning, the gap between what they believed and what the oil market believed closed violently, in their favor.

I think they are the most underrated forecasters in finance, and the mechanics of what they do explain more about how the world actually runs than any central bank speech you will read this year.

The clause

Start with a fact that surprises almost everyone who learns it: no navy closed the Strait of Hormuz this spring. No blockade was declared. What closed the strait, in the operational sense that mattered, was an insurance clause.

Nearly every merchant ship on earth carries war-risk insurance, and nearly all of it is written or reinsured through the Lloyd's market in London, which handles an estimated 70 to 80 percent of global marine war cover. Buried in those policies is a mechanism of quiet, absolute power: when underwriters designate a stretch of water as a listed high-risk area, coverage there can be cancelled or repriced on seven days' notice. Not renegotiated at the annual renewal. Seven days. At the peak of the crisis this spring, underwriters stopped quoting fixed terms entirely and moved to pricing Gulf transits day by day, which is the actuarial equivalent of a doctor refusing to give a prognosis beyond tomorrow.

So picture the decision that actually keeps a tanker at anchor. No admiral weighs geopolitics anywhere near it. A shipowner with a $110 million vessel listens to a broker explain what this week's cover costs, and does division.

Before the war, hull war cover for a seven-day Gulf transit ran about 0.25 percent of the vessel's insured value. For a large crude carrier worth $100 to 120 million, call it $250,000 to $300,000 per trip. A real cost, but a rounding error against a cargo of two million barrels.

At the peak this spring, the same seven days of cover reached 1 percent of hull value. One million to $1.2 million. Per transit. Each way.

Do the arithmetic slowly, because this is the part I find beautiful. An insurance premium is a probability wearing a dollar sign: the underwriter's estimate of the chance of losing the ship, times the cost of the ship, plus a margin for being wrong. When the market charges 1 percent of a vessel's value for one week of exposure, it is telling you it puts the odds of catastrophe for that ship, that week, somewhere near one in a hundred. For context, the ordinary total-loss rate in commercial shipping is measured in hundredths of a percent per year. The underwriters were pricing a single lap through Hormuz as roughly a thousand times more dangerous than a normal year at sea.

Nobody at Lloyd's held a press conference to announce this. They just quoted the number, and the number did the governing. Owners who wouldn't pay it anchored their ships outside the Gulf; at the worst point, some 80 million barrels sat queued in and around the strait, waiting for paper. Oil, it turns out, flows at the speed of documents.

There is a strategic insight buried here that the war coverage keeps missing. Iran understood this system perfectly. You do not need to sink many tankers to close the world's most important waterway. You need to sink approximately one, credibly threaten a second, and let the seven-day clauses do the rest. The mines and drones were, in a sense, inputs to an actuarial model in London, and the model was always going to be the thing that shut the door. Insurance is the transmission mechanism between violence and commerce, and it transmits fast.

The two guilds

Which brings me to the disagreement, the one that resolved itself at $78 this morning.

Through late June, the oil futures market unwound the entire war premium. Brent closed at $72.68 on June 25, below where it stood the day before the first strike in February. The strip looked at the ceasefire memorandum, the resumed tanker traffic, the 20 million barrels exiting the strait in a single day, and concluded: over.

The insurance market looked at the same strait and declined to agree. Premiums came off their peaks as traffic resumed, but underwriters kept Hormuz listed, kept the short-notice machinery armed, and kept pricing Gulf transits at multiples of the old baseline. The industry's own explanation, which I'd frame as a philosophy of knowledge disguised as a business practice, is that war-risk pricing normalizes months after the politics, because underwriters do not accept announcements as evidence. They want sustained, boring proof of safety: weeks of vessel-tracking data showing transits completing, cargoes discharging, nothing exploding. A ceasefire, to an underwriter, is a hypothesis. A thousand uneventful voyages are a fact.

Think about why the two guilds diverge. Intelligence has nothing to do with it; the difference is the shape of what they sell. An oil futures trader who is wrong about peace loses a spread; he marks to market every day and can reverse in seconds. An underwriter who is wrong about peace loses the whole ship. One of them can afford to trade the announcement. The other can only afford to trade the evidence. When you want to know what's actually true about a dangerous place, ask the person who has to pay for the hull, whole, on the day it disappears.

Yesterday Iran fired on three tankers, and the underwriters' epistemology won the argument. The strip repriced six months of geopolitics in one session. The war-risk market barely had to move. It had never left.

A few other readings from this morning's tape, quickly, because they'll matter in the coming weeks. Gold fell 2.2 percent, to $4,066, on a morning when missiles were flying, which sounds impossible until you remember that on the worst days investors sell what they can, to cover what they must; the safe asset becomes the ATM. Hold that thought, because gold in 2026 is a stranger story than it looks, and I'll come back to it in a few issues. Bitcoin, which its adherents spent years billing as the ultimate crisis asset, sat at $61,900, having spent the year proving it trades like a leveraged tech stock with opinions. And the sharpest equity losses this morning were nowhere near the Gulf: Seoul, down 5.35 percent, because South Korea imports roughly 70 percent of its crude from the Middle East and runs on the assumption that the strait is a fact of nature rather than a policy.

What to watch instead of the news

The practical takeaway is a habit. For the rest of this war, and honestly for every conflict after it, skip the headlines about ceasefires and read the insurance signals instead. They are public, they are numerical, and they are set by people who are ruinously punished for optimism.

The specific tell: the day hull war cover for a Hormuz transit gets quoted back at 0.25 percent, on fixed terms rather than day rates, the war is over, whatever the communiqués say. Underwriters will get there only when the tracking data forces them to, which means that number cannot be spun, lobbied, or announced into existence. It is the closest thing this conflict has to an honest referee.

We are, for the record, nowhere near it. As of this morning the quotes are moving the other way, the seven-day notices are going out, and the queue outside the strait has started growing again. The last time the underwriters and the futures market disagreed, it took the strip three months and a $47 round trip to catch up to what London already believed.

The bookmakers set the odds. The underwriters decide whether the game gets played at all. This morning they suspended play, quietly, seven days at a time, and my strong advice is to believe them over every printed word out of Washington and Tehran combined, including, obviously, mine.

Sources: Al Jazeera and Fortune reporting, July 8, 2026 (strikes, tanker incidents, market moves, Trump remarks); Lloyd's market and war-risk pricing data via marine insurance trade coverage, 2026 (premium levels, seven-day notice mechanics, Lloyd's-Chubb $400M consortium, Gulf barrel queue); EIA and exchange data for the June price path as covered in the July 1 issue.

item.title: Conceived in Debt
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: On the evening of June 20, 1790, Thomas Jefferson hosted a small dinner at his rented house on Maiden Lane in New York.
item.content:encoded:
On the evening of June 20, 1790, Thomas Jefferson hosted a small dinner at his rented house on Maiden Lane in New York. Two guests: Alexander Hamilton and James Madison. Hamilton arrived desperate. His plan for the federal government to assume the states' unpaid war debts, about $25 million, the load-bearing wall of his entire financial architecture, was dying in Congress. Madison was the one killing it.

By dessert they had a deal. Madison would stop whipping votes against assumption. In exchange, the new national capital would go south, to a swamp on the Potomac. The United States got its debt plan and Virginia got Washington, D.C., and if you ever want to explain American politics to a foreigner, you can do worse than: we put the capital where it is as part of a debt restructuring.

Today the republic turns 250. The debt Hamilton consolidated came to roughly $75 million. The debt outstanding this morning is a touch under $40 trillion. Call it a 530,000-fold increase, against a population that grew 85-fold. And the fact I want to dwell on is stranger than either number: for the entire 250 years, someone respectable has been announcing that the debt is about to ruin us, the ruin has never arrived, and yet the people saying it this year might finally have a point. Not because the number got big. The number was always big. Because of who has quietly stopped showing up to lend.

Since it is a birthday, let's open the gifts. Who actually holds the IOUs of the United States?

Start with the strangest chunk: about $8 trillion, a fifth of the gross figure, the government owes to itself. Social Security collects payroll taxes, doesn't need all of them yet, and parks the surplus in Treasury securities, because the law says it must. One drawer of the federal dresser holding a note from another drawer. Economists argue about whether this even counts as debt. My favorite way to think about it: a family that keeps its vacation savings in a jar, borrows from the jar for groceries, and leaves a note. The note is real. The family's total wealth is unchanged. But the vacation still has to be paid for, and the note-writer and the jar-owner are, awkwardly, the same person at different ages. That $8 trillion is a promise from present taxpayers to future retirees with extra paperwork.

Now the $21 trillion or so held domestically outside the family jar. The Federal Reserve holds about $4.5 trillion, the residue of crisis-era bond buying that it has been letting shrink for years. Mutual funds hold about $5.2 trillion, which very much includes you, if you have a 401(k) with a target-date fund: some slice of your retirement is a loan to the Treasury, whether or not you've ever thought of yourself as a bond investor. Commercial banks hold about $2.1 trillion. Pension funds another $1.1 trillion. State and local governments, $1.6 trillion. Insurers, corporations, households directly, a few trillion more. The largest creditor of the United States, by an enormous margin, is Americans.

That is the origin of the old comfort, "we owe it to ourselves." Which is about one-third true. The other roughly 32 percent of the marketable stuff is held abroad, and it is inside that 32 percent that the actual 2026 story lives.

Japan is the largest foreign creditor, at about $1.2 trillion. Second place is the United Kingdom at $889 billion, though "the United Kingdom" here mostly means the City of London, hedge funds and asset managers custodying bonds for clients from everywhere, finance's equivalent of a mail-forwarding address. And China, which for most of my adult life was the boogeyman of every debt polemic, the creditor who supposedly had America by the throat: $683 billion. Third place, and shrinking.

Read that again, because the polemics haven't updated. China held around $1.3 trillion at the peak, in 2013. It has since let nearly half of that roll off, methodically, year after year, without drama, replaced at the margin by gold in the People's Bank vaults. The creditor everyone feared didn't dump the bonds. It just stopped renewing them, the way you quit a gym: no announcement, you just don't go back.

Which brings us to the machine itself, because "the debt" is mostly misunderstood as a pile when it is actually a conveyor belt.

The United States never repays its debt. This scandalizes people, and it shouldn't; no large country repays its debt, any more than a bank "repays" its depositors all at once. What the Treasury does is roll it. Bonds mature constantly, every week, and the Treasury pays them off by selling new bonds to whoever shows up at that week's auction. The average maturity of the whole book is about six years. Hamilton's original insight, the one he traded a capital city for, was exactly this: a sovereign debt is never really a sum owed, it is a relationship with a market, and the only thing that matters is that the market keeps answering the phone.

So the real exposure is never the principal. Nobody will ever knock on the door asking for the $40 trillion. The exposure is the rate at which the conveyor belt gets refinanced. Old debt issued in the 2010s and early 2020s carries coupons of 1 and 2 percent. Every week, a slab of it matures and gets reissued at today's rates, which are 4-something on the short end and pushing 5 on the long end. The blended interest rate on the whole book grinds upward mechanically, a mortgage that refloats itself in slow motion, and there is nothing any Congress can do about the part that has already happened.

Here is where the numbers stop being trivia. Net interest is running at about $1.1 trillion a year. That is 19 cents of every dollar of federal revenue, before the government buys a single aircraft carrier, processes a single Social Security check, or pays a single park ranger. It exceeds the defense budget. In March the total crossed $39 trillion; the pace of accumulation works out to about $90,000 per second, which means that in the twelve or so minutes it takes to read this essay, the republic will have borrowed roughly another $65 million, about what Hamilton assumed from all thirteen states combined, adjusted for nothing, because adjustment would ruin a perfectly good sentence.

And this year's deficit will run past $2 trillion in peacetime. Except, of course, it is not exactly peacetime. There was a war this spring; wars cost money and suppress nobody's spending. The Supreme Court in February struck down the tariff program that was supposed to bring in hundreds of billions, and the Treasury now owes importers refunds instead. Revenue lighter than promised, spending heavier than planned, on a book that reprices itself upward every week. That is the fiscal picture on the country's 250th birthday.

Now, the case for calm, because there is one, and it has won the argument for 250 straight years. The United States borrows in a currency it prints. It cannot be forced into the kind of default that ruined Argentina; the machine can always technically pay. American debt is the world's savings mattress: when anything anywhere goes wrong, money runs toward Treasuries, a reflex demonstrated as recently as March, when a literal war in the Persian Gulf sent buyers into the very bonds funding the belligerent. The republic has carried debt loads that looked apocalyptic before: 106 percent of GDP in 1946, worked off over three decades through growth and inflation without a single missed coupon. Anyone who bet on American fiscal collapse at any point since Maiden Lane has lost, and most of them lost embarrassingly.

The bears' problem was never the arithmetic. It was the tense. The debt is unsustainable, they say, and the market hears: not today, then, and goes back to lunch.

But something has changed, and the number's size is the wrong place to look for it. Look instead at the composition of the people at the auctions.

For decades the marginal buyer of Treasuries was, in one costume or another, someone who had to buy. Foreign central banks recycling trade surpluses, because where else do you put a trillion dollars. The Fed, buying by the trillion to fight crises. Pension funds matching liabilities under rules that treated Treasuries as the risk-free default. Price-insensitive, all of them. They didn't ask what the yield was. They asked how much was available.

That cast is retiring. China: down $600 billion from peak and still drifting away. The Fed: shrinking its holdings on schedule, a seller in net terms. The trade surpluses that needed recycling: smaller, and increasingly recycled into gold instead, which is a sentence that would have sounded medieval in 2015 and is now simply a fact of reserve management. Who replaced them? Mutual funds, hedge funds, households, the London custody chain. Investors, in other words. People who compare yields, read Congressional Budget Office reports, and can leave.

The debt didn't change. The lender did. The mortgage analogy from earlier needs its final turn: the house never mattered, and even the size of the mortgage never quite mattered, so long as the bank was your uncle. The bank is no longer your uncle. It is a fund manager in London with a Bloomberg terminal and no particular feelings about the Fourth of July.

None of this produces a crisis on a schedule, and I am not predicting one; the honest record of debt-doom predictions is 0 for 250, and humility is warranted. What a buyer rotation produces instead is a price. Investors who can leave don't storm out; they ask for more yield, a quarter point here, a half point there, a weak auction that "tails" on a Tuesday afternoon nobody remembers. The bill for 250 years of it-always-works arrives as a rate. There is never a bang.

So here is the marker I'll put down on the republic's birthday. Ignore the debt-clock billboards; the number will cross $40 trillion soon and the billboard will not tell you anything the $39 trillion didn't. Watch the 30-year bond instead. The 30-year is the pure expression of the question who wants to lend America money for a generation, at what price, with no obligation to say yes. If the buyer rotation I've described is real, it will show up there first, as a yield that grinds toward and then through 5 percent and stays there even on the days when stocks wobble and money is supposed to hide in bonds. That is the tell. The short end belongs to the Fed. The long end belongs to the willing.

Two hundred fifty years ago the country's first Treasury Secretary bet the capital city on a simple proposition: that the United States, if it paid reliably, would never run out of willing lenders. He was right for longer than any financial forecast in recorded history. He also wrote, in a line his fans quote less often, that a national debt would be a blessing only "if it is not excessive."

He never defined excessive. He didn't have to. The auctions define it, one Tuesday at a time.

Sources: Joint Economic Committee monthly debt updates (totals, accumulation rate); CRS RS22331, Foreign Holdings of Federal Debt (April 2026 update); Peter G. Peterson Foundation interest tracker (net interest, share of revenue); Treasury TIC and SIFMA holder data (spring 2026 releases); Compromise of 1790 per Jefferson's memoranda; Hamilton, First Report on Public Credit (January 1790) and letter to Robert Morris (April 30, 1781).

item.title: The War the Oil Market Stopped Pricing
item.dc:creator: Umang
item.description: On February 27 of this year, a barrel of Brent crude cost about $72.
item.content:encoded:
On February 27 of this year, a barrel of Brent crude cost about $72. Last Thursday, June 25, it cost $72.68.

Between those two prices there was a war. There is still a war, or at least a 60-day pause with a war attached to both ends of it. Iranian missiles, American carrier groups, a mined Strait of Hormuz, gasoline at $3.99 a gallon, diesel at $5.40, emergency cabinet meetings on four continents. Brent went through $100 in the second week of March and at the worst printed within a dollar of $120. And then, over three months, the entire thing was unwound, dollar by dollar, until the price arrived back where it started, like a tide going out and taking the evidence with it.

If you fell asleep on February 27 and woke up last week and looked only at the oil price, you would conclude that nothing had happened.

Something happened. So the interesting question, the one I want to spend the next few thousand words on, is what exactly the oil market thinks a war is. Because whatever it thinks, it is plainly something different from what the rest of us think, and the difference is one of the more useful things you can understand about how prices work.

What the market saw

Quick reconstruction, for anyone who spent the spring under professional obligations to look away.

The war began on February 28. Within days, the Strait of Hormuz, the 21-mile-wide channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil transits, was under a de facto closure. Not an announced closure with a press release. Mines, drones, and insurance rates did the closing. Tankers idled. Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE shut in production, because pumping oil you cannot ship is a hobby, and these are commercial operations.

The price did what you'd expect. Brent had started the year around $61. It ended February at $72 as the buildup got loud. Then March: through $100, a spike to nearly $120, retail gasoline in America at its highest real price in over two years by month-end. The US Energy Information Administration later noted, with the placid tone of an agency that files its panic under appendices, that strong domestic inventories and planned releases from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve helped limit the damage on the American side.

One detail from that stretch tells you more than the headline price, and I keep returning to it. At the start of the year, Brent (the global, seaborne benchmark) traded about $4 above WTI (the American, landlocked one). By March 31 the gap was $25. The average spread for March was $11, the widest in over five years.

Stop on that for a second. Crude oil is crude oil. A refinery does not check a barrel's passport for sentimental reasons; it checks because location is the product. In March, the same fungible molecule was worth $25 more if it happened to be floating near Rotterdam than if it was sitting in a tank in Cushing, Oklahoma. The war exposed something more useful than a higher oil price: the fact that there is no such thing. There are prices of oil in places, and a chokepoint is a machine for prying those prices apart. America, pumping 13-plus million barrels a day at home, an ocean away from the mines, was suddenly an island, and island economics are their own economics.

The other tell was the shape of the futures curve, which most news coverage skips because curves don't photograph well. During the worst of it, the front of the curve was screaming while the back of the curve yawned. Oil for delivery next month went vertical; oil for delivery in 2028 barely moved. Depending on which contract month you squinted at, "the oil price" at the end of March was anywhere from $104 to $118. That gap between the front and the back is the market saying something specific: we have a problem today, and we do not believe we will have this problem for long.

Hold that thought, because the market turned out to mean it.

The bookmaker

The mental model I'd offer comes with a warning: I'm going to push it until it breaks, because the place where it breaks is the actual point of this essay.

The oil futures market is a bookmaker, and it is pricing a fight.

A bookmaker does not set odds by deciding who deserves to win. He does not price outrage, or history, or whose cause is just. He prices flows. Money on one side, money on the other, and the line moves until the flows balance. When commentators say a market is "complacent" about a war, they are usually making a category error. The market is not offering an opinion about the war. It is offering a price at which barrels change hands, and barrels, unlike opinions, can be counted.

So price a war the way the bookmaker would. A war matters to the price of oil through exactly one channel: barrels that would have reached buyers, and don't. Everything else (the rhetoric, the strikes on things that are not oil infrastructure, the terrifying maps on television) is noise, in the strict sense that it does not subtract barrels. The March spike was the market's estimate of subtracted barrels: probability of disruption, times size, times duration. Something like an insurance premium, recalculated every second.

And then, from late March onward, each component of that premium got marked down in public.

Demand did some of the work. Gasoline at $3.99 is its own quiet policy intervention. People drive less, airlines trim schedules, factories in price-sensitive countries slow down. Nobody votes on it, it just happens, a few hundred thousand barrels a day of consumption evaporating because the price told them to.

Inventories did more of the work. The world, it turns out, keeps a pantry. Commercial tanks, strategic reserves, oil sitting in ships. When the strait shut, the world did not stop eating; it ate from the pantry. The EIA credited American inventories and SPR plans with capping the domestic spike, and every other consuming nation was doing a version of the same thing.

Then, decisively, the barrels came back. By late June, tanker traffic through Hormuz was approaching pre-war volumes, with at least 20 million barrels exiting the strait in a single 24-hour window. Oman opened temporary shipping corridors. The Gulf producers that had shut in production, for want of any way to ship it, began reversing course, and the market started sniffing a further twist: Iran itself, under temporary sanctions relief attached to the talks, positioned to sell more oil into the recovery, its own war financed in part by the reopening it had been threatening.

And there was, of course, the ceasefire itself. On June 17 the parties signed a 14-point memorandum, brokered with Pakistani mediation, that set a 60-day negotiating window; on June 22, in Switzerland, negotiators agreed a roadmap toward a final deal. Mines still need clearing, and full normality in the strait is reckoned in weeks. Iran spent last Thursday warning against "unauthorized" crossings, which is the kind of thing you say when you want everyone to remember you could change your mind.

Add it up the way the bookmaker does. Fewer barrels lost than feared, ample barrels stored, barrels returning faster than expected, and a signed piece of paper suggesting the whole thing winds down. The line moves. $119 becomes $95 becomes $80 becomes, by June 25, $72.68: the pre-war price, exactly. The odds have gone back to the pre-fight line. The market has priced the war at zero.

There is even a small flourish in the curve to confirm it. August Brent closed that day at $72.68 while September closed at $73.59. The front month cheaper than the next one, a mild contango, is the market's way of saying near-term supply is ample. Four months ago the curve was inverted and shrieking. Now it slouches. Markets do not do relief rallies in oil; they do boredom, and boredom, in this market, is a price signal with real information in it.

Where the pantry analogy breaks

I promised the model would break. Here is where.

A bookmaker settles his book when the fight ends. The oil market's fight has not ended. It has a tarp over it, and the tarp has a date printed on it. The 60-day clock in the June 17 memorandum runs out in mid-August. As of today, that is about 47 days away. The market is treating the deadline as scenery. Deadlines are scenery, right up until they are cliffs.

And the pantry problem is worse than the price implies, which is the part I find under-discussed to the point of negligence. The world got through March, April, and May by eating stored barrels: commercial inventories drawn, strategic reserves committed, OPEC's shut-in capacity absorbing the shock in both directions. Those buffers are how a fifth of the world's seaborne oil supply got interrupted and the whole episode ended up costing drivers a bad spring rather than a global recession.

But a pantry, once eaten, is not a pantry. It's shelving.

Refilling takes months at best. Strategic reserves are refilled at political speed, which is slower than any other speed known to engineering. Shut-in production comes back, but Gulf spare capacity, the famous cushion that market coverage invokes like a superstition, has already been partly converted from cushion into supply. Run the same shock again in the autumn, against drawn inventories and thinner spare capacity, and the same barrels-times-duration arithmetic produces a very different price path. The first spike was absorbed by buffers built over years. The second one would land on the shelving.

Which brings us to the strangest thing about $72.68. It is the same price as February 27, but it is describing a different world. February's $72 had a full pantry behind it and no war. June's $72.68 has a depleted pantry, a mined strait being swept, a signed memorandum with 47 days on the clock, and a regional order held together by negotiators in Switzerland. The number is identical. The situation the number claims to summarize is not even similar. If you want a one-sentence education in the limits of price as information, there it is: price is a summary statistic, and like all summary statistics it achieves its tidiness by throwing information away.

The people closest to the physical trade are not acting bored, incidentally. Somewhere in the strait this week, crews are sweeping for mines so that a tanker can load on schedule, and the tanker is loading on schedule because a memorandum says the missiles will stay in their tubes for another few weeks. Every quoted price you see rests on an assumption that thousands of such people, none of whom you will ever hear named, keep succeeding at their jobs. The screen shows $72.68. The screen is very confident. The minesweepers are still out there, which tells you what the people who handle the actual barrels think confidence is worth.

What I'd actually take from this

Two things, and then a marker you can hold me to.

The first is a reading habit. When a geopolitical shock hits a commodity, ignore the level and read the spreads: the gap between benchmarks (Brent minus WTI told you March's true story better than either price alone), and the gap between the front and back of the curve. The level tells you that people are scared. The spreads tell you where the barrels aren't, and how long the market expects the problem to last. All the actual information density lives in the differences.

The second is about what "the market has priced it in" means. Nobody concluded the war is over. The current flow of barrels, adjusted by the current stock of buffers, simply stopped justifying a premium. That is a statement about logistics, with a time horizon of weeks, and it carries no warranty beyond that horizon. Treating a logistics verdict as a geopolitical forecast is how people got surprised in February, and I suspect it is how some people will get surprised again.

So, the marker. The strip is pricing peace as the base case: not as a hope, as a base case, at full weight, with the pantry thin. If the mid-August deadline passes into a real agreement, oil in the 60s is defensible and this essay becomes a curiosity. If the talks fail with the buffers where they are, the next spike starts from a weaker floor than February's and travels further. I don't know which it will be, and neither does the strip; the difference between us is that the strip is obligated to pick a number anyway, and it has picked one that assumes the tarp holds.

$72.68 is the market's way of saying the fire is out. What the market means is that the fire is under a tarp, the extinguishers are half-empty, and everyone has agreed to check back in August.

Certainty is the one commodity the Gulf has never exported. It is currently trading at par.
